formulations.label: Tablets
formulations.note: The clinic stocks 10 mg tablets. No UK SmPC for a 10 mg norethisterone tablet was found on emc or MHRA Products, so this entry uses UK 5 mg tablet SmPCs. Doses below are written in mg. Where a UK SmPC says '1 tablet', that means 5 mg, not one 10 mg tablet; a 5 mg dose cannot be given as a whole 10 mg tablet.

src.q: Norethisterone 5mg Tablets 2. Qualitative and quantitative composition Norethisterone 5.0mg.
Each tablet contains 5 milligrams of norethisterone BP.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Low dose: dysfunctional uterine bleeding, polymenorrhoea, menorrhagia, metropathia haemorrhagica, premenstrual syndrome, postponement of menstruation (one UK SmPC also endometriosis and dysmenorrhoea). High dose (generic 5 mg SmPC only): disseminated breast carcinoma.

src.q: At low dose: Dysfuntional uterine bleeding Polymenorrhoea Menorrhagia Metropathia Haemorrhagia Pre-menstrual syndrome Postponement of menstruation At high dose: Disseminated carcinoma of the breast.
Metropathia haemorrhagica. Premenstrual syndrome. Postponement of menstruation. Endometriosis. Menorrhagia. Dysmenorrhoea.

items.t: SPS: norethisterone is the only progestogen licensed in the UK to delay periods.

src.q: Norethisterone is the only progestogen licensed in the UK to delay periods.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPCs or SPS page accessed.

items.t: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding, polymenorrhoea, menorrhagia, metropathia haemorrhagica: 5 mg three times daily for 10 days; to prevent recurrence, 5 mg twice daily on days 19-26 of the next two cycles.

src.q: 1 tablet three times daily for 10 days; bleeding usually stops within 48 hours.
One tablet twice daily, from days 19 to 26 of the two subsequent cycles, should be given to prevent recurrence of the condition.

items.t: Postponement of menstruation: 5 mg three times daily, starting 3 days before the expected period. One UK SmPC: continue for no longer than 10-14 days. SPS: can be taken for up to 3 to 4 weeks if necessary.

src.q: Postponement of menstruation: 1 tablet three times daily, starting three days before the expected onset of menstruation.
continuing for not longer than 10 to 14 days
Norethisterone can be taken for up to 3 to 4 weeks if necessary.

items.t: Endometriosis: generic SmPC 5 mg three times daily for at least 6 months (increase to 20-25 mg daily if spotting); another UK SmPC starts 5 mg twice daily from day 1-5 of the cycle for 4-6 months.

src.q: Endometriosis: 1 tablet three times daily for a minimum treatment period of six months. The dosage should be increased to 4 or 5 tablets a day if spotting occurs.
Treatment should begin between the first and 5th day of the cycle with 1 of tablet Primolut N twice daily.

items.t: Premenstrual syndrome: generic SmPC 5 mg daily on days 16-25; another UK SmPC 5-15 mg daily on days 19-26, repeated for several cycles.

src.q: Pre-menstrual syndrome: 1 tablet daily from days 16 to 25 of the menstrual cycle.
may be relieved by the administration of 1-3 tablets daily from the 19th to the 26th day of the cycle

items.t: Disseminated breast carcinoma (generic SmPC): start 40 mg daily, increasing to 60 mg daily if no regression.

src.q: For disseminated breast carcinoma the starting dose is 8 tablets (40mg) per day increasing to 12 tablets (60mg) if no regression is noted.

items.t: One UK SmPC: not intended for use in children.

src.q: Not intended for use in children.

items.t: Both UK SmPCs: hypersensitivity; pregnancy; previous idiopathic or current venous thromboembolism; active or recent arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g. angina, myocardial infarction); history in pregnancy of idiopathic jaundice or severe pruritus; undiagnosed genital/vaginal bleeding.

src.q: Previous idiopathic or current venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism) Active or recent arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g. angina, myocardial infarction)
History during pregnancy of idiopathic jaundice Severe pruritus or pemphigoid gestationis Undiagnosed irregular vaginal bleeding Porphyria

items.t: Generic 5 mg SmPC also: disturbance of liver function; porphyria.

src.q: Disturbance of liver function

items.t: Another UK SmPC also: breastfeeding; prodromi of thrombosis (e.g. TIA, angina); high risk of venous or arterial thrombosis; migraine with focal neurological symptoms; diabetes with vascular involvement; severe hepatic disease until liver values are normal; previous or existing liver tumours; known, past or suspected sex-hormone-dependent malignancy; untreated endometrial hyperplasia.

src.q: 3. Lactation.

6. Presence or a history of prodromi of a thrombosis (e.g. transient ischaemic attack, angina pectoris). 7. A high risk of venous or arterial thrombosis (see section 4.4) 8. History of migraine with focal neurological symptoms. 9. Diabetes mellitus with vascular involvement.
10. Presence or history of severe hepatic disease as long as liver function values have not returned to normal. 11. Previous or existing liver tumours (benign or malignant).
12. Known, past or suspected sex hormone-dependent malignancies, including of the genital organs or breast cancer.
15. Untreated endometrial hyperplasia.

items.t: If no menstrual bleeding follows a course, exclude pregnancy before another course.

src.q: the possibility of pregnancy must be excluded before a further course is given

items.t: Stop if jaundice or worsening liver function, a significant rise in blood pressure, or new migraine-type headache occurs.

src.q: Therapy should be discontinued if the following occur: - Jaundice or deterioration in liver function - Significant increase in blood pressure - New onset of migraine-type headache

items.t: Fluid retention: special care in epilepsy, migraine, asthma, cardiac or renal dysfunction.

src.q: Special care should be taken when prescribing norethisterone in patients with conditions which might be aggravated by this factor: - Epilepsy - Migraine - Asthma - Cardiac dysfunction - Renal dysfunction

items.t: VTE: personal or strong family history of thromboembolism should be investigated for thrombophilia; until evaluated or anticoagulated, treat progestogens as contraindicated. Consider stopping 4-6 weeks before elective surgery with expected prolonged immobilisation; stop if VTE develops.

src.q: Until a thorough evaluation of thrombophillic factors has been made or anticoagulant treatment initiated, use of progestogens in these patients should be viewed as contraindicated.
consideration should be given to stopping progestogen therapy 4-6 weeks pre-operatively
If VTE develops after initiating therapy the drug should be withdrawn.

items.t: Sudden visual impairment, proptosis, diplopia or migraine: ophthalmological assessment before continuing. Very rarely, hepatic adenoma.

src.q: Any patient who develops an acute impairment of vision, proptosis, diplopia or migraine headache should be carefully evaluated ophthalmologically
In very rare cases, hepatic adenomas may be associated with progesterone-only pill (POP) use.

items.t: Enzyme inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin, St John's wort; generic SmPC also lists tetracyclines, ampicillin and co-trimoxazole) may increase progestogen metabolism and reduce levels.

src.q: These compounds include anticonvulsants (e.g., phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine) and anti-infectives (e.g., rifampicin, rifabutin, nevirapine, efavirenz, tetracyclines, ampicillin, oxacillin and cotrimoxazole)
Herbal preparations containing St John's wort ( Hypericum perforatum ) may induce the metabolism of progestogens. Progestogen levels may therefore be reduced.

items.t: Special care with other drugs that cause fluid retention, such as NSAIDs and vasodilators.

src.q: Special care should be taken when progestogens are administered with other drugs which also cause fluid retention, such as NSAIDs and vasodilators.

items.t: Already on anticoagulants: weigh risks and benefits of progestogen therapy carefully.

src.q: Where a patient is already taking anticoagulants, the risks and benefits of progestogen therapy should be carefully considered.

items.t: One UK SmPC: CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole), verapamil, macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin) and diltiazem can increase progestin levels; clinical relevance unknown. Ciclosporin levels may rise; lamotrigine levels may fall.

src.q: Strong and moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals (e.g. itraconazole, voriconazole, fluconazole), verapamil, macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin, erythromycin), diltiazem and grapefruit juice can increase plasma concentrations of the estrogen or the progestin or both.
The clinical relevance of potential interactions with enzyme inhibitors remains unknown.

items.t: Progestogens can affect some laboratory tests (liver function, thyroid function, coagulation).

src.q: Progestogens can influence certain laboratory tests (e.g., tests for hepatic function, thyroid function and coagulation).

items.t: No dose advice. Renal dysfunction: special care because of fluid retention.

src.q: 3. Lactation.
Primolut N can pass into breast milk and therefore should be avoided during lactation.

items.t: Not a contraceptive: use another method of contraception to avoid pregnancy when delaying periods (SPS).

src.q: The individual should be advised that norethisterone is not a contraceptive and so another form of contraceptive should be used to avoid pregnancy.

items.t: At 5-10 mg norethisterone suppresses ovulation.

src.q: Norethisterone given at intermediate doses (5-10mg) suppresses ovulation via its effect on the pituitary.

items.t: Frequencies are not given in the UK SmPCs checked. Reported effects include breakthrough bleeding, spotting, amenorrhoea, breast tenderness, headache, nausea, fluid retention and weight gain.

oedema/fluid retention, bloating, weight gain
galactorrhoea, mastodynia, tenderness
depression, headache, dizziness, fatigue
nausea, vomiting, cholestatic icterus/jaundice

items.t: Thromboembolic disorders, cerebral and myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, retinal thrombosis: if VTE develops, stop. Patients should contact a doctor at once with leg swelling, sudden chest pain or breathlessness.

src.q: thrombo-embolic disorders, cerebral and myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, increased blood pressure, palpitations, pulmonary embolism, retinal thrombosis
Patients should be advised to contact their doctor immediately if they become aware of a potential thromboembolic symptom (e.g., painful swelling in the leg, sudden pain in the chest, dyspnoea).
